title: Take any four digits, repeat one simple step, and you land on 6174
body: Pick any four-digit number whose digits aren’t all the same. Arrange the digits from largest to smallest, then from smallest to largest, and subtract the second from the first. Repeat with the result. Within **seven rounds** you always reach 6174, and from there the step gives 6174 forever. Indian mathematician D. R. Kaprekar published this oddity in 1955, and 6174 has been called Kaprekar’s constant ever since.

slides.alt: Animated amber seven-segment display: 3524 is sorted into 5432 and 2345 and subtracted, giving 3087, then 8352, then 6174, which gives 6174 again. Six more starting numbers reach 6174 in 1 to 7 steps, and a bar graph of all 8,991 four-digit numbers shows none needs more than 7.

steps.label: Pick four digits, not all the same
Subtract the second from the first
Within seven rounds the answer is 6174

slides.heading: Why it works
slides.text: The result depends only on which digits you hold, not on their order, so after the first step only 54 different numbers can come up. All 54 funnel down into one fixed point. Three-digit numbers have their own: 495.

slides.heading: The fine print
slides.text: If the digits are all the same, like 1111, the step gives 0 and the trick stalls. Keep leading zeros when you sort, so 3087 becomes 8730 − 0378. Every other four-digit number arrives at 6174 in at most seven steps.

slides.prompt: Start from 2025. How many steps to 6174?

slides.clue: The Indian mathematician who published the 6174 routine in 1955; the constant bears his name
slides.detail: 6174 is Kaprekar’s constant. Three-digit numbers have their own: 495.
